overview: Euoplocephalus tutus was the most completely known ankylosaurid — a heavily armoured tanklike dinosaur from the Campanian of Alberta (~76–75 Ma), about six metres long. Every part of its body, including the eyelids, was armoured with fused bony plates. Its large tail club, formed by fused vertebrae and surrounded by massive bony knobs, could generate forces sufficient to break the fibula of a large theropod.

Euoplocephalus is known from over 40 specimens across multiple formations, making it the most commonly found ankylosaurid in North America. Despite this abundance, most specimens are disarticulated — the heavy, dense body tends to sink and disarticulate in water — and a complete skeleton in natural articulation has not yet been found.

fossilSites.note: Campanian deposits with the most abundant Euoplocephalus material; multiple specimens from different quarries across the formation.

articles.title: Discovery and abundance
articles.body: Named by Lambe in 1910 from Dinosaur Park Formation material. Over 40 specimens are now referred to the genus, making it the best-represented ankylosaurid. Multiple specimens of different sizes allow study of ontogenetic changes in armour arrangement. The bony eyelids (ossified eyelids) are a distinctive feature preserved in several specimens.

articles.title: Tail club biomechanics
articles.body: The tail club is formed by two large bony knobs (osteoderms) fused to the distal tail vertebrae, which are themselves fused into a rigid handle. Computer modelling of the tail musculature shows that the club could be swung laterally with forces sufficient to cause serious injury to a theropod's leg bones. The club was clearly an active weapon — the tendons attaching to the handle region are strongly developed.

articles.title: Armour function
articles.body: Euoplocephalus armour covers the dorsal and lateral surfaces with large keeled scutes, smaller flat ossicles, and a complex arrangement that varied regionally on the body. The underbelly was less well protected — exposed if the animal were flipped. The armoured eyelids are unique features that protected the eyes during confrontation. The overall armour system combined passive protection with the active weapon of the tail club.

record.description: Euoplocephalus tutus was an ankylosaurid from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta and Montana. Multiple skulls and partial skeletons document a broad, armoured quadruped with a tail club, but modern revision removed many historic specimens into Anodontosaurus, Dyoplosaurus and Scolosaurus.
facts: No one specimen preserves the complete armour layout.
The tail club is real, while its behavioural use is inferred biomechanically.
Taxonomic revision greatly reduced the geographic and temporal range once attributed to Euoplocephalus.

presentation.heroLead: A broad, low-slung armoured dinosaur with a bony tail club from Alberta, known from several skulls and partial skeletons once that name had been stripped of the many specimens it used to absorb.

animalParagraphs: Euoplocephalus was a heavily armoured, four-legged plant-eater of the ankylosaurid group that lived in what is now Alberta, and probably Montana, during the late Campanian. It was around five to six metres long, with a wide, flat body carried on short limbs and a tail ending in a heavy bony club.

Its skull was broad and short, roofed with fused plates of bony armour, with small horn-like bones at the rear corners and even bony eyelids. Rows of keeled osteoderms covered the neck, back and tail, the largest arranged in half-rings around the neck. The teeth were small and leaf-shaped, and the nasal passages inside the skull followed a looping course.

For most of the twentieth century almost every ankylosaurid skeleton from Alberta was called Euoplocephalus, making it seem one of the best-known armoured dinosaurs. A 2013 revision reassigned many of those specimens to Anodontosaurus, Dyoplosaurus and Scolosaurus, leaving a smaller but still substantial sample from the Dinosaur Park Formation.
animalHighlights: A broad skull capped with fused armour plates, with bony eyelids that could close over the eyes.
Half-rings of large keeled osteoderms around the neck and a tail ending in a solid bony club.
The historic catch-all genus for Alberta ankylosaurids, cut down to a smaller core sample by modern revision.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by teeth and skull shape
lifeCards.reason: Small leaf-shaped teeth, a broad beak and a wide, low skull fit a low-level browser on soft vegetation. No gut contents are known for the genus.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Short, stout limbs and a broad pelvis from partial skeletons indicate a slow, four-legged gait; speed is inferred from proportions.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: No fully complete individual is described, and some historic large skeletons now belong to other genera; length and mass are estimates.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Individual osteoderms and neck half-rings are directly preserved, but no single specimen shows the complete armour arrangement, and colour is unknown.

locality.note: The holotype was collected by Lawrence Lambe in 1897 from the Belly River beds, now the Dinosaur Park Formation. Some material from the Judith River Formation of Montana has also been referred to the genus.

presentation.classificationSummary: Euoplocephalus is an ankylosaurine ankylosaurid, part of the club-tailed armoured dinosaurs of Late Cretaceous North America. It is closely related to Anodontosaurus, Scolosaurus and Dyoplosaurus, the genera into which many of its former specimens were moved.

related.reason: Compare with the larger, younger relative from the very end of the Cretaceous.
Compare with a duck-billed dinosaur that browsed the same Late Cretaceous plains at greater height.
Compare with the tyrannosaurid predator that shared the Dinosaur Park Formation.

questions.title: Which old specimens still belong here?
questions.copy: Skulls and armour that once defined Euoplocephalus have been redistributed among several genera, and a few historic specimens without diagnostic skulls remain hard to place.

questions.title: How was the armour arranged?
questions.copy: Osteoderms are known from many individuals, but no single Euoplocephalus skeleton preserves the full pattern in place, so reconstructions borrow from relatives.

questions.title: How was the tail club used?
questions.copy: The club is real and biomechanical models suggest it could deliver damaging blows, but whether it was used against predators, rivals or both is not directly recorded.

review.ageReviewNote: Restricted mainly to the Dinosaur Park Formation, about 76.5-74.4 Ma, rather than an 80-66 Ma composite range.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.note: A partial skull roof and a cervical half-ring of armour collected by Lawrence Lambe in 1897 and named Stereocephalus tutus in 1902; renamed Euoplocephalus in 1910 because the original name was preoccupied.

specimens.name: Referred skull and skeleton
specimens.institution: American Museum of Natural History, New York
specimens.note: A skull with associated postcranial material and armour from the Dinosaur Park Formation, retained in Euoplocephalus by the 2013 revision.

specimens.name: Referred skull
specimens.note: A well-preserved skull used in cranial redescriptions of the genus.

panel.headline: Several skulls and partial armoured skeletons, after revision trimmed the sample.
panel.standfirst: Euoplocephalus rests on a fragmentary holotype and a set of referred skulls and partial skeletons from the Dinosaur Park Formation. The sample is smaller than the historic literature suggests, because many former specimens are now assigned to other ankylosaurid genera.

coverage.label: Good
coverage.basis: Skulls, armour, vertebrae, girdles and limbs are all represented across referred specimens, but no individual is complete and the full armour layout is not preserved in place.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: A holotype skull roof and neck half-ring, several complete or near-complete referred skulls, and partial skeletons with vertebrae, ribs, girdles, limbs, osteoderms and tail-club material.
knownRemains.note: Because the holotype is so incomplete, referral of skeletons depends on skull features, and specimens without skulls are difficult to assign with confidence.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: The holotype skull roof plus several referred skulls with fused cranial armour, braincases, bony eyelids, mandibles and teeth.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal vertebrae, including the fused handle vertebrae of the tail club, from partial skeletons.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Pelvic and pectoral girdle elements and limb bones from referred skeletons; complete hands and feet are rare.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Numerous osteoderms and cervical half-rings, some found in association; no skin impressions, colour or gut contents are securely attributed to the genus.

specimenCards.title: CMN 0210 · holotype
specimenCards.description: A partial skull roof and a cervical half-ring found by Lawrence Lambe in 1897 and named in 1902. Its fragmentary nature is the root of a century of taxonomic confusion around Alberta ankylosaurids.
specimenCards.meta: Red Deer River · Dinosaur Park Formation · Canadian Museum of Nature

specimenCards.title: AMNH 5405 · skull and skeleton
specimenCards.description: A skull with associated postcranium and armour that anchors much of the modern understanding of the genus, retained in Euoplocephalus when many other New York and Ottawa specimens were reassigned.
specimenCards.meta: Dinosaur Park Formation · American Museum of Natural History

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Fused cranial armour, bony eyelids, teeth, neck half-rings, isolated osteoderms, tail-club elements and partial postcranial skeletons.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A slow, low-browsing armoured herbivore whose tail club served as a weapon, and whose former specimens represent several coexisting ankylosaurid genera.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: The complete in-place armour pattern, the assignment of some historic skeletons, how the tail club was used, and colour and skin texture.
